title: Why static friction beats kinetic friction
description: A block resists starting to slide harder than it resists continuing to slide, because the microscopic welds holding two surfaces together get stronger the longer they sit still.

## TL;DR

Pushing a heavy box, the hardest moment is the instant before it starts to move. Once it's sliding, less force keeps it going. The reason is time: two stationary surfaces touch at microscopic points that behave like tiny cold welds, and those welds strengthen the longer they sit undisturbed. Sliding keeps breaking and remaking them too fast for that strengthening to happen, so kinetic friction is almost always weaker than static friction, for the same two surfaces.
:::

## Contact is a handful of welds, not a surface

However flat two surfaces look, they touch only at the tips of microscopic bumps, asperities, and the [module on why broken solids cannot re-bond](atomic-cohesion-and-fracture.qmd) already gives the number: the real contact area is $A_{\text{real}} = F_N / H$, the normal force divided by the material's hardness, typically under $0.01\%$ of what the surfaces appear to cover. Everywhere else, the surfaces are tens to hundreds of nanometres apart, held apart by their own roughness.

At those few real contact points (Figure 1), the local pressure is enormous, close to the material's yield strength, because all of the applied force is funnelled through a tiny area. Under that pressure the asperity tips deform plastically and, for many material pairs, form genuine adhesive junctions: small, cold-welded bridges, exactly the mechanism the cold-welding module describes at full scale in vacuum, happening in miniature on every surface you touch. Friction, in this picture, is the force needed to shear those junctions apart. The classical adhesion theory of friction, developed by Bowden and Tabor, puts it plainly: friction force is proportional to real contact area times the shear strength of the junction material, not to the surfaces' apparent size, which is exactly why Amontons' observation that friction is independent of apparent contact area and proportional to normal force holds up so well.

## Standing still lets the welds cure

A junction that has just formed is weak. Left alone under load, it gets stronger: the asperity tips continue to creep and flow plastically for a period after first contact, growing the real contact area, and for many materials the adhesive bond itself strengthens as more atoms settle into intimate contact, not unlike letting glue cure rather than testing it the instant it's applied. This time-dependence is well documented in friction experiments, most systematically in rock mechanics, where Dieterich showed that the peak static friction of two rock surfaces increases roughly logarithmically with how long they've been held in stationary contact before being forced to slip. Wait longer before pushing, and it takes more force to get the same two surfaces moving.


## Sliding never lets a junction age

Once the applied force exceeds the maximum static friction, $F_{s,\max} = \mu_s F_N$, the aged junctions shear apart and the surfaces begin to slide. From that point on, the physics changes. A moving surface is constantly bringing fresh, unweathered asperities into contact and shearing them apart again within microseconds, far too quickly for the creep and adhesion strengthening described above to take hold. The average junction the sliding surface encounters is younger and weaker than the aged junctions that had to be broken to start the motion, so less force is needed to sustain the sliding, $F_k = \mu_k F_N$, than was needed to start it: $\mu_k < \mu_s$. Figure 2 puts the whole sequence on one plot.

Textbook tables put rough numbers on the gap. Dry steel on steel is commonly listed around $\mu_s \approx 0.74$ and $\mu_k \approx 0.57$; dry rubber on concrete around $\mu_s \approx 1.0$ and $\mu_k \approx 0.8$. For a $50\text{ kg}$ steel block on a steel floor, that's the difference between needing about $363\text{ N}$ to break it loose and only about $280\text{ N}$ to keep it sliding, a drop of roughly $23\%$ the instant it starts moving. Push with exactly the force that kept it sliding a moment ago, applied to a block still at rest, and it won't move at all; that jump between the two regimes is exactly what your hand feels as the "give" the instant a stuck object breaks free.

It's worth being honest about the limits of this picture. Amontons' and Coulomb's friction "laws," including $\mu_k < \mu_s$, are excellent approximations for many everyday material pairs, dry metals, wood, most rubbers on hard surfaces, but they are empirical rules, not exact physics. The gap between static and kinetic friction depends on surface finish, contamination, humidity and temperature, and it shrinks or occasionally vanishes for some material pairs and lubrication conditions. When it doesn't vanish, and the static-to-kinetic transition happens repeatedly and rapidly, you get stick-slip: the surface sticks while a driving force builds toward $F_{s,\max}$, breaks free and slides until it slows enough to stick again, over and over. That's the mechanism behind a squeaking door hinge, a bowed violin string, and brake squeal.

## Key takeaways

- Two surfaces touch only at microscopic asperity tips; friction is the force needed to shear the adhesive junctions those tips form, not a property of the visible surface.
- Junctions strengthen the longer two surfaces sit in stationary contact, through continued plastic creep and adhesion; static friction rises with contact time.
- Sliding constantly replaces junctions faster than they can age, so kinetic friction is set by fresh, weak junctions rather than aged, strong ones, giving $\mu_k < \mu_s$.
- This asymmetry is an empirical regularity, not a universal law; it varies by material pair and can produce stick-slip motion when a surface repeatedly catches and releases.
